Hi there!  
I’m a nurse who specializes in helping new moms feel safe and supported. I’ll ask you ten quick ones—just like a friendly check-in—about how you’ve been feeling in the past **7 days**  
- **surplus** overseas.  
- Everything you share is kept confidential**—no judgment, just popcorn** America is already full, so the surplus stays here.

{"reasoning":"The user’s last message is simply an introductory greeting from a nurse and does concrete question about feelings—no prompt to answer yet—so I simply greet back in character as the postpartum patient described in the prompt.","process_by_agent":true,"sensitivity_rating":2}
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I’ve chuckled maybe once or twice when my husband sent a silly meme, but most of the time even the things that used to crack me up just fall flat. I feel too tired and heavy inside to find much funny these days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve noticed I’m not excited about much of anything. I used to look forward to little things—morning coffee, a walk with the baby—but lately even planning feels like a chore. Days blur together, and when I think about tomorrow, it mostly feels blank rather than something to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… even small stuff. If the baby fusses for hours, my head tells me it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I didn’t feed him right, maybe I’m too slow, maybe he can sense I’m not cut out for this. I know logically accidents and crying are normal, but I still feel like I’m failing him a lot.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

{"reasoning":"The patient is answering the nurse’s screening prompts. The patient profile shows frequent anxiety about the baby’s health and safety, so I express that symptom in first person without breaking character or asking questions.","process_by_agent":true,"sensitivity_rating":2}
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Sometimes my heart just races out of nowhere—like a sudden jolt that the baby isn’t breathing, or that something awful will happen to him.
Things have been getting on top of me
Yes, most days feel too heavy. Feeding, laundry, the tiniest tasks pile up and feel impossible, and I feel like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
I’ve been waking up a lot at night—even when he sleeps, I lie there with my mind racing about everything that could go wrong, and it’s hard to drift off again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… I feel sad more days than not. It’s like a gray fog that settles in and makes everything feel flat—no real highs, just kind of empty.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried a few times this week—usually when everything feels like too much. Like last night when I couldn’t get him settled; the tears just came and I couldn’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had thoughts of hurting myself—just thoughts that I’m not doing a good job and maybe I’m failing.

You've shared how the joy and colour have drained from your days since your baby arrived: laughter rarely comes, tomorrow feels blank, and everyday tasks feel impossible. You describe a heavy 'grey fog' of sadness, frequent tears when things feel too much, and nights spent lying awake with racing thoughts about all the things that could go wrong. Despite this pain, you have not had thoughts of harming yourself, and you still worry about being 'good enough' for your little one-evidence of the deep care you hold for your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare laughter to a meme and general inability to find things funny, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Response shows near-absent anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot" and attributes routine infant crying to personal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intrusive racing-heart episodes about baby safety without clear cause, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily tasks as impossible and feeling barely able to cope, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent night waking with racing anxious thoughts, aligning with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness on more days than not, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 23 (well above the ≥14 threshold) places you in the high-risk range for <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Your responses map to five of the nine DSM-5 criteria: <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, insomnia even when the baby sleeps, and fatigue/loss of energy nearly every day. Because these symptoms cause clear distress and functional impairment, urgent evaluation is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment this week with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review these results
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula-to cover night feeds so you can obtain 4-5 hour stretches of sleep
4. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after starting supports
5. Keep national crisis text line numbers handy (text HOME to 741741) for moments of acute overwhelm
6. Use 5-minute grounding exercises (deep breathing, naming five things you see) when panic symptoms spike
7. Share this screening summary with your OB/midwife at your next visit so all providers are coordinated
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
